title: The Lightest Way Down a Triangle

concept.title: Work from the bottom row upwards: each number picks the smaller of two numbers below it
body: Numbers are arranged in a triangle: 1 number in the first row, 2 in the second, and so on. You start at the top and walk down; from a number in row `i` at position `j` you may step to position `j` or `j + 1` of the next row. The cost of a walk is the sum of the numbers on it. Find the **smallest** cost of a walk from the top to the bottom row. For the triangle `2 / 3 4 / 6 5 7 / 4 1 8 3` the best walk 2 + 3 + 5 + 1 costs 11.

Going from the top is awkward, because the number of walks grows fast and each cell is reached from different directions. Go from the **bottom** instead. Let `best(i, j)` be the smallest cost of a walk that starts at the cell `(i, j)` and ends at the bottom. For the last row it is the number itself. For a higher row the walk steps to one of the two cells below, so **`best(i, j) = value(i, j) + min(best(i + 1, j), best(i + 1, j + 1))`**. The answer is `best(0, 0)`.

body.code:
row = [the last row of the triangle]
for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):             # from the second last row up to the top
    for j in range(i + 1):
        row[j] = tri[i][j] + min(row[j], row[j + 1])
print(row[0])

body: The values arrive as one long list, so the row `i` starts at the index `i * (i + 1) / 2`. One array of length `n` is enough, because the row above needs only the row below it, and we overwrite from left to right (a cell reads `row[j]` and `row[j + 1]`, which are not changed yet). The time is O(n^2), the memory O(n). **Reversing the direction** of a DP is a useful trick: a state defined by "from here to the end" often needs fewer special cases than "from the start to here".

statement: A triangle has `n` rows; the row `i` (counting from 1) has `i` numbers. You start at the single number in the top row and repeatedly step to one of the two numbers directly below (the same position or the next one to the right) until you reach the bottom row. Print the smallest possible sum of the numbers on such a walk.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `m`: the number of rows of the triangle and the number of values in it (`m = n * (n + 1) / 2`).
The second line has the `m` values: the first row (1 value), then the second row (2 values), and so on up to the row `n` (`n` values).
hints: Let best(i, j) be the smallest cost of a walk from the cell (i, j) to the bottom.
In the last row it is the value itself; above it is the value plus the smaller of the two cells below.
Row i starts at the index i * (i + 1) / 2 of the list; a single array of length n is enough.

starter.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, m = map(int, input().split())
tri = list(map(int, input().split()))

# Your code here

explanation: Starting from the last row, every number is replaced by itself plus the smaller of the two numbers below it, so that best(i, j) is the smallest cost of a walk from that cell to the bottom; the top value is the answer. One array of length n is reused for all rows.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n, m = map(int, input().split())
tri = list(map(int, input().split()))

start = (n - 1) * n // 2
row = tri[start:start + n]
for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
    base = i * (i + 1) // 2
    for j in range(i + 1):
        row[j] = tri[base + j] + min(row[j], row[j + 1])
print(row[0])
